item.text:
**Verdict**
Mixed, leaning negative. Srettha did make a few durable, rule-based moves in rights and humanitarian administration, but the evidence is thin relative to the question, and most of what exists is either rhetoric or narrow legalization rather than broad institution-building that clearly outlived his personal rule.

**Accepted Claims**
- **Title:** Statement of Prime Minister at the Summit for Democracy  
  **Publisher:** Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Kingdom of Thailand  
  **Date:** March 20, 2024  
  **URL:** https://www.mfa.go.th/en/content/summit-for-democracy-statement-2024?cate=5d5bcb4e15e39c3060006848  
  **Summary:** Srettha framed governance around democracy, rule of law, human rights, Universal Health Coverage, Education for All, and marriage equality. This is useful as intent evidence for institution-building, but it is still mostly rhetoric rather than proof of durable institutional change.  
  **Question IDs:** 6B.9, 6B.8

- **Title:** Thailand ratifies disappearance convention, backs anti-torture law  
  **Publisher:** Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Kingdom of Thailand  
  **Date:** May 16, 2024  
  **URL:** https://www.mfa.go.th/en/content/icpped140524-2?page=5d5bd3da15e39c306002aaf9  
  **Summary:** This is the clearest concrete institutional reform I found: a formal legal safeguard against torture and enforced disappearance. It is durable on paper and not dependent on Srettha personally day-to-day.  
  **Question IDs:** 6B.9, 6B.8, 6B.6

- **Title:** Thailand’s House passed Marriage Equality Act  
  **Publisher:** Human Rights Watch  
  **Date:** March 27, 2024  
  **URL:** https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/03/27/thailand-promptly-pass-same-sex-marriage-bill  
  **Summary:** Thailand advanced a major equal-status reform for LGBT people through legislation, which is one of the stronger durable social-institution wins of 2024. It goes beyond aggregate welfare and creates a legal structure that survives any one leader.  
  **Question IDs:** 6B.9, 6B.8

- **Title:** Thailand’s Senate approves same-sex marriage bill  
  **Publisher:** Human Rights Watch  
  **Date:** June 18, 2024  
  **URL:** https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/06/18/victory-same-sex-marriage-thailand  
  **Summary:** The final Senate approval strengthened the durability of the marriage-equality reform. This is the best evidence that Srettha helped carry a rights reform into law rather than just issuing a temporary executive gesture.  
  **Question IDs:** 6B.9, 6B.8

- **Title:** Thailand used Red Cross and AHA Centre channels for cross-border aid  
  **Publisher:** Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Kingdom of Thailand  
  **Date:** March 26, 2024  
  **URL:** https://www.mfa.go.th/en/content/vfm260324-2?cate=5d5bcb4e15e39c306000683e  
  **Summary:** The government ran border relief through the Thai Red Cross, Myanmar Red Cross, local communities, and AHA Centre technical support. That is evidence of a more institutional, less patronage-driven humanitarian delivery model.  
  **Question IDs:** 6B.9, 6B.6, 6B.7

- **Title:** Thailand coordinated with UN agencies to upscale border assistance  
  **Publisher:** Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Kingdom of Thailand  
  **Date:** April 26, 2024  
  **URL:** https://www.mfa.go.th/en/content/vfm-chairs-hm-asst-mtg-260424-2?cate=5d5bcb4e15e39c306000683e  
  **Summary:** Coordination with UNHCR, UNICEF, WFP, UNDP, and ICRC suggests a professional, multi-actor humanitarian system rather than a personalized or loyalty-based one. This is stronger on durable process than on any single policy announcement.  
  **Question IDs:** 6B.9, 6B.6, 6B.7

- **Title:** Thailand: New Government Slow to Protect Rights  
  **Publisher:** Human Rights Watch  
  **Date:** January 11, 2024  
  **URL:** https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/01/11/thailand-new-government-slow-protect-rights  
  **Summary:** HRW said the government had not undertaken serious rights reforms and was still pursuing politically motivated prosecutions of protesters and monarchy critics. That cuts against a claim that Srettha was building durable institutions that reliably constrained abuse.  
  **Question IDs:** 6B.9, 6B.7, 6B.8

- **Title:** Thailand: ‘Swap Mart’ Targets Foreign Dissidents, Refugees  
  **Publisher:** Human Rights Watch  
  **Date:** May 15, 2024  
  **URL:** https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/05/15/thailand-swap-mart-targets-foreign-dissidents-refugees  
  **Summary:** HRW described harassment, surveillance, forced returns, and deportations without due process. This is negative evidence because it shows state capacity still being used in ways that are not durable rights institutions.  
  **Question IDs:** 6B.9, 6B.8, 6B.7

- **Title:** Thailand: Rights Activist Shot Dead in Deep South  
  **Publisher:** Human Rights Watch  
  **Date:** June 26, 2024  
  **URL:** https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/06/26/thailand-rights-activist-shot-dead-deep-south  
  **Summary:** This does not show a direct Srettha order, but it points to continuing fragility in the southern border region, where long-running abuses and weak protection remained unresolved. That undercuts any claim of durable institutional repair in marginalized areas.  
  **Question IDs:** 6B.9, 6B.8, 6B.6

- **Title:** Thailand | Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism  
  **Publisher:** Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism  
  **Date:** June 17, 2024  
  **URL:** https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/digital-news-report/2024/thailand  
  **Summary:** The report says Thai media could still criticize policy, but self-censorship, elite constraints, and fear around military and lèse-majesté issues remained strong. That suggests the information ecosystem was not being durably depersonalized or institutionalized.  
  **Question IDs:** 6B.9, 6B.8, 6B.7

- **Title:** Thailand’s leaders shun UN human rights chief  
  **Publisher:** Human Rights Watch  
  **Date:** June 6, 2024  
  **URL:** https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/06/06/thailands-leaders-shun-un-human-rights-chief  
  **Summary:** HRW said senior Thai officials avoided meeting the UN high commissioner for human rights, apparently to avoid scrutiny. That is negative evidence for durable oversight culture and institutional openness.  
  **Question IDs:** 6B.9, 6B.8

**Search Gap**
I did not find strong direct evidence that Srettha built broad, durable social institutions in health, education, social insurance, civil service, anti-corruption enforcement, or local-government administration. Most positive evidence is limited to:
- one clear legal rights reform area,
- one anti-abuse treaty step,
- and a more professional humanitarian delivery channel around the Myanmar border.

What is missing is a visible, repeatable reform record that would clearly survive personal turnover. The negative side is also real: politically motivated prosecutions, weak rights protection, and avoidance of external scrutiny suggest that institutional durability remained limited.
